body:
YES — verified against the paper and frozen release, with a custody caveat.

The paper states that all data and materials generated or analyzed are available in the authors GitHub repository. The archived v1.0.0 release is Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17467024 and Git tag v1.0.0 resolves to commit dbe49b37173864ae0432233e67e3732a5979c88b. Its tree contains:

- 60 participant recall transcript text files under data/recall/transcripts, plus processed recall CSVs;
- human, GPT, and LLaMA segmentation CSVs under data/segmentation;
- the three approximately 1,500-word Born a Crime excerpts under data/stories;
- Python and RMarkdown analysis code.

The authors README makes a reproducibility limitation explicit: regenerated LLM segmentations may differ, outputs were manually reformatted for the RMarkdown analyses, and the release does not provide one linear raw-narrative-to-final-plot pipeline. Therefore exact reanalysis of published processed tables, regeneration from scripts, and our independent benchmark are three different receipts.

Availability is not authorization to copy the texts into this repository. The top-level MIT license does not establish redistribution rights for third-party memoir excerpts, and under storymodel4s policy participant recall text remains barred until the owner records an REB basis for redistribution. We can run the comparison in an authorized external environment and retain code, hashes, aggregate results, and receipts here after review. I did not download or import any study data.

Primary sources:
https://www.nature.com/articles/s44271-025-00359-7#data-availability
https://github.com/ryanapanela/EventRecall/tree/v1.0.0
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17467024
